newsitem.title: ITALY: Bank of Italy cuts rates to 20-year low.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Italy cuts rates to 20-year low.

text.p: The Bank of Italy, encouraged by moderate inflation, said on Tuesday it would cut the official discount rate to 6.75 percent from 7.50 percent -- the lowest level for over 20 years.

The move, eagerly awaited by financial markets, came as a relief to Prime Minister Romano Prodi's government which was anxious for a fall in borrowing costs to help lower the interest bill on Italy's huge public debt.
The Bank of Italy said it would cut the discount rate on Wednesday and would simultaneously lower the fixed term advances, or Lombard rate, to 8.25 percent from a previous 9.00 percent.
It was the third rate reduction in six months and the discount rate's lowest level since September 1975. The last monetary easing came on October 23.
"The decision by the Bank of Italy will give a new impulse to development and the economic pick-up as well as employment in the country," a statement from Prodi's office said.
The Bank of Italy said it acted following a steady decline in inflation in recent months.

Earlier on Tuesday preliminary data from 11 Italian cities pointed to the inflation rate rising 2.6 percent year-on-year in January, unchanged from the last two months. The central bank has said it wants to bring average inflation this year to under 3.0 percent from 3.9 percent in 1996.
The bank said in a statement it was closely watching trends in consumer demands, labour costs and price policies.

While the market had expected further rate cuts, the exact timing surprised many analysts who did not think the Bank of Italy would move until after a long-running pay dispute in the large metalworkers and engineering sector was resolved.
"I didn't expect the Bank to cut just on January CPI data which were really neutral," said Gianluca Sanna, economist with Banco di Sardegna in Milan.
"The Bank is clearly not afraid of possible inflationary pressures from labour costs," he added.

The easing was good news for the Prodi government which has pinned much of its hopes on lower interest rate bills as it tries to whip the economy into shape for the planned launch of the single European currency in 1999.

The government estimates that it saves 20 trillion lire ($12.6 billion) a year in debt servicing costs for every percentage point fall in the discount rate, once the cut has fully worked its way into the system.
The Treasury spent some 195 trillion lire on interest last year, ensuring the state ran up a hefty budget deficit.
Treasury Minister Carlo Agzelio Ciampi expressed satisfaction on Tuesday over the rate cut. "This way there are grounds for a stable and lasting economic recovery," he said in a statement.
Analysts predicted further monetary easing in the months ahead, with the inflation outlook positive and no signs that the economy is about to take off.
"We expect another cut in the next quarter -- of around the same size," Paolo Casadio, macroeconomist at bank Credito Italiano told Reuters Financial Television. $1 = 1,582 lire
